record.paper_title: Recent advances in open billiards with some open problems
record.original_question: Does every triangular billiard contain at least one periodic orbit, and more generally does every polygonal billiard contain at least one periodic orbit when arbitrary directions of motion are allowed?

evidence.quote: Open problem 5. Existence of periodic orbits: Do all triangular (or more generally polygonal) billiards contain at least one periodic orbit?
Note that this admits arbitrary directions; it is easy to construct rational polygonal billiards for which a particular directional flow is never periodic.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A polygonal billiard is the dynamical system describing the motion of a point particle inside a planar polygon $P$: the particle travels in straight lines at unit speed and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) at the boundary, with trajectories that hit a vertex being undefined. A trajectory is called periodic if, after finitely many reflections, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial direction of motion.

Prove or disprove the following statements:

(a) Every triangle $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ admits at least one periodic billiard trajectory.

(b) More generally, every simple polygon $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ admits at least one periodic billiard trajectory.

Here arbitrary initial directions of motion are allowed (the question is not about a fixed directional flow; for rational polygons one can construct directions whose flow has no periodic orbits, but this does not preclude the existence of periodic orbits in some other direction).
artifact.status_search_result: The existence of a periodic billiard orbit is classically known for rational polygons and for acute and right triangles (Fagnano's orbit and its analogues). For obtuse triangles, R. E. Schwartz proved that every obtuse triangle whose largest angle is at most 100° has a periodic orbit, and computer-assisted work has pushed this bound further (towards roughly 112.5°), but the general case for arbitrary obtuse triangles, and a fortiori the case of arbitrary simple polygons, remains open as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: Obtuse Triangular Billiards II: 100 Degrees Worth of Periodic Trajectories
status_evidence.snippet: Schwartz proves every obtuse triangle with largest angle at most 100 degrees has a periodic billiard path.
status_evidence.claim: Partial result: periodic orbits exist for all triangles with largest angle ≤ 100°.

status_evidence.title: Survey Lecture on Billiards (Schwartz, ICM)
status_evidence.snippet: The triangular billiards conjecture — every triangle has a periodic billiard orbit — is widely believed but unproven for general obtuse triangles.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture remains open in general.

status_evidence.title: Open problems in billiards and quantitative symplectic geometry
status_evidence.snippet: Lists existence of periodic orbits in polygonal billiards as an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: Listed as an open problem in a 2026 survey.
